newsitem.title: USA: Airport anti-terror measures stall in Senate.
newsitem.headline: Airport anti-terror measures stall in Senate.

text.p: A wide-ranging aviation bill stepping up airport security against terrorist attacks was blocked in the U.S. Senate on Friday, effectively stalling any action on the bill until next year.
Wisconsin Democratic Sen. Russell Feingold objected to taking up the bill, complaining it contained a special interest provision designed to prevent Federal Express employees from forming a union.

Feingold's move effectively blocked action on the bill, which passed the House of Representatives earlier Friday. Because Congress was expected to adjourn in the next few days, the bill was likely to be shelved for the year.

"The provision makes a significant change in federal law to give Federal Express an edge in its current attempt to stop some of its employees from forming a union ... that's the issue, let's just get that out of here," Feingold said.

Among the anti-terorrism provisions were requirements that airlines do background checks on employees screening passengers, baggage and cargo and that the Federal Aviation Administration certify security firms doing the screening.

The bill also established rules for record-setting flights stemming from the crash of a plane this year in which 7-year-old Jessica Dubroff was killed while trying to become the youngest pilot to fly across the country.
The rules would bar anyone without a valid pilot's certificate and medical certificate from handling the controls of a plane while trying to set a record.

Also in the measure were reforms of the way airlines deal with families of crash victims. They were taken from a separate bill drafted after complaints by families of victims of the July 17 TWA 800 crash off Long Island, New York.

The provision regarding Federal Express would allow reclassifying employees under the Railway Labor Act rather than the National Labor Relations Act. The change, which would require employees to organize nationally rather than being allowed to organize locally, would make it more difficult for them to strike.
